blocks.text: But I, wretched woman, have perished because of the owls, which were always hooting in the night watches. And Aelian, Hist. book 1, ch. 29, on the owl: Νύκτωρ μὲν ἀγρυπνεῖ· [Nyktōr men agrypnei] By night it keeps awake. And of the same bird Varro, De ling. Lat. book 4: By night it sings and keeps awake. With this in view, then, the Psalmist says: I have watched, and was like a solitary bird upon the roof. Some, however, refer this to the sparrow, as though it kept awake for fear, which Suidas has from Theodoret. But you will read nothing of the kind in those who have written on the nature of birds. And those who keep sparrows at home know that they sleep at night, like all birds except the nocturnal ones. Otherwise, since they are awake by day, they would never sleep at all. Moreover, צפור בודד, a solitary bird, is rightly said of the eagle-owl or the owl, because it lives in desert places, as was said in the preceding verse. Hence Damir: وكنية الانثي ام الخراب [wa-kunyat al-unthī umm al-kharāb] And the female (owl) is surnamed mother of desolation. And further on: البوم اصناف وكلها تهب الخلوة بانفسها والتفرد [al-būm aṣnāf wa-kulluhā thb al-khalwa bi-anfusihā wa-l-tafarrud] There are several species of owls, all of which love seclusion and solitude. Therefore, just as the wild ass is called בודד boded, that is, solitary, in Os. VIII, 9., because it dwells in the wilderness, by the same reasoning the eagle-owl or owl is here rightly called צפור בודד, bird boded, that is, solitary, since it nests in places very far removed from human traffic. Accordingly Pliny, book 29, ch. 4, mocking the magi who prescribe remedies for the hair from the egg of the eagle-owl, says: Who, I ask, could ever have seen an eagle-owl's egg, when to have seen the bird itself is a por- [col. 155] tent? And Alcamus on الصدي [al-ṣadā], that is, the eagle-owl: طاير يصر بالليل يقفر قفرانا [ṭāyir yaṣirr bi-l-layl yaqfur qafrānan] It is a bird that shrieks at night and lives in desert [II, 732] places. Indeed, to this point belongs the fact that in Arabic it is called صدي tsada, as in Chaldee צדיא tsadja. For צדו tsadu or צדות tsaduth means to the Chaldeans waste, desolation; and the verb צדה tseda means to be laid waste, to be made desolate. In this sense it is used in the Niphal by Zephaniah, ch. 3, v. 6. Thus from the very name which the Chaldeans, Syrians and Arabs gave the eagle-owl, you may infer that it is a solitary bird, living in desolate places. But the eagle-owl is also called a solitary bird because it is not a gregarious animal but one that wanders alone. Hence the Poet, in book 4 of the Aeneid:
And the eagle-owl alone on the rooftops with funereal song was seen to lament, and to draw out its long notes into weeping.

But why should the sparrow be called solitary, since it is a gregarious bird and nests under the roofs of houses? I admit that within the sparrow kind some are wild. Hence Alexander of Myndus teaches, in Athenaeus book 9, δύο γένη εἶναι τῶν στρουθῶν, τὸ μὲν ἥμερον, τὸ δὲ ἄγριον [dyo genē einai tōn strouthōn, to men hēmeron, to de agrion], that there are two kinds of sparrows, one domestic, the other wild. But wild sparrows do not betake themselves to the roofs of houses, as does the bird of which the Psalmist speaks, whom he describes upon the roof. Therefore, if a sparrow is meant, it cannot be the wild sparrow but only the domestic one. They answer that the domestic sparrow is called solitary because it has been bereaved of its mate. This might be tolerable if the sparrow, like the turtledove or the dove, remained widowed after losing its spouse. But sparrows live by other customs: it is a most lustful animal, so given to Venus that it covers the female, if not a hundred times, as the Arabs report, at least seven times in an hour. Hence the poets yoke it to the chariot of Venus. Bound by no law, then, it rushes into promiscuous love and has no fixed spouse. So, as it was never a husband, neither does it become a widower. That is why the books of the Philosophers say nothing of a solitary sparrow. And those err by the whole breadth of heaven who derive the French name of the sparrow from the Greek μόνιος [monios]. For μόνιος [monios] is an epithet of the boar, not of the sparrow. And to us moineau is something quite different, namely μοναχίσκος [monachiskos], monachulus [little monk]. By this name the male is called, because, like monks, it seems to be hooded. Something else again is the passer solitarius [solitary sparrow] of the people of Trent. For it belongs not to the sparrows but to the blackbird kind, which the Philosopher describes as βαιὸς [baios], dusky, and ἐπὶ τῶν πετρῶν, καὶ ἐπὶ τῶν κεράμων τὰς διατριβὰς ποιῶν [epi tōn petrōn, kai epi tōn keramōn tas diatribas poiōn], living on rocks and roof-tiles. So this is nothing to the point. Now if you ask why the Psalmist describes a nocturnal bird, say the eagle-owl or the owl, upon the roof, the answer is ready. For although eagle-owls and owls nest in desert places, yet at night they are accustomed sometimes to come to towns and cultivated places and to sound their funereal song from the roofs and gables of houses. There is no one who has not heard this at some time. So nothing is more frequent in the poets. Ovid, Metam. book 6, Fable 7:
[II, 733] — — — — and on the roof the unholy eagle-owl brooded, and sat on the gable of the bridal chamber.
The nocturnal eagle-owl sat on the opposite gable.
